title: Military Housing: Undoing a Costly Deal and Fixing Decades of Neglect
label: 10 September 2026 · Armed forces housing
summary: MPs examined how a 1996 decision to sell thousands of military family homes left taxpayers an estimated £14.5 billion worse off by 2024, and whether the Ministry of Defence can now repair the damage. The committee praised the £6 billion deal to buy back more than 36,000 homes but challenged officials over poor housing conditions, slow repairs and the decision to delay some planned spending. Officials outlined a £9.2 billion, ten-year programme to improve military homes, alongside plans to build new housing and establish a dedicated Defence Housing Service. The central concern was whether the department has the money, expertise and urgency to deliver better homes for military families while avoiding another expensive mistake.

glossary.definition: The UK government department responsible for the armed forces, including military buildings and housing.
The private property company that bought thousands of military homes in 1996 and rented them back to the Ministry of Defence.
The independent public body that examines how the UK government spends public money.
An accounting rule that requires organisations to record many long-term rental commitments as financial liabilities.
A set of minimum requirements for housing condition, safety, facilities and reasonable warmth.
Military housing provided to individual service personnel rather than families.
The planned public organisation responsible for managing, improving and developing military housing.
A planning agreement under which property developers may be required to provide affordable homes or other local benefits.
Proposed legislation concerning the armed forces, including legal powers to establish the Defence Housing Service.
A government organisation providing specialist financial and commercial advice on public assets and major transactions.

chapters.title: 1. How the original deal went wrong
chapters.takeaway: The 1996 sale brought in money immediately but left the government paying rent on homes it no longer owned, while giving it little reason to invest in them.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: In 1996, the Ministry of Defence sold around 55,000 military family homes to Annington Homes for £1.7 billion. It then rented them back. The National Audit Office estimates that by 2024, the decision had left the government £14.5 billion worse off than if it had kept the properties. We've now bought back more than 36,000 homes for £6 billion. How did we get into this position?

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: Our service personnel risk their lives for this country, and we've let them down financially and through the condition of their homes. Why did the government agree to such a poor contract in the first place?

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: We need to distinguish between the original sale, which was a bad deal, and the recent repurchase, which I believe was a good one. We wouldn't make the 1996 deal today. The government then wanted to raise money through a competitive sale, partly to improve housing, although only a small proportion of the proceeds actually went towards improvements. The central lesson is that government must protect the long-term value of important public assets, rather than concentrate on immediate financial returns.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: But this was an extraordinary commitment, including leases lasting 999 years. Surely someone should have questioned whether it made sense. Who negotiated it, and why did it take so long to challenge?

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: Financial analysis was very different in 1996. We didn't have today's specialist government organisations to help assess deals, and our methods for testing financial assumptions were less developed. I haven't personally reviewed the original advice, so I can't give a detailed judgment about every decision made then. But today's approach puts far more emphasis on expert scrutiny, uncertainty and checking the assumptions behind long-term agreements.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: The arrangement also seems to have rewarded Annington when the government improved the houses. Even though taxpayers paid for the improvements, the company could benefit from higher rents or increased property values. Is that right?

turns.speaker: Mike Green
turns.text: Yes. We were responsible for maintaining houses we didn't own. If we improved a property, it became more valuable and we could end up paying more rent for it. The original calculations also assumed extremely low growth in property values over time. Those assumptions turned out to be a major problem. We have much stronger requirements for checking financial estimates today.

turns.speaker: Rupert Pearce
turns.text: The rent was below the normal market rate partly because the Ministry of Defence had to pay for maintenance. But that created the wrong incentives: we carried the costs of improvements while the owner could benefit from their value.

turns.speaker: Chris Kane
turns.text: I'm concerned that we're treating this as simply a different way of thinking in 1996. The deal seems particularly bad even by the standards of the time. Have we properly examined what actually went wrong, rather than just relying on the fact that modern procedures are better?

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: I've identified several lessons: understanding what assets are worth, examining hidden assumptions, testing what happens if circumstances change, and involving outside experts. The objectives given to officials also matter. In 1996, those objectives encouraged a shorter-term approach than was appropriate. We need to make long-term care of public assets an explicit priority.

turns.speaker: Chris Kane
turns.text: The military studies history to learn lessons, often going much further back than 30 years. I think it's reasonable to expect the Ministry of Defence to do the same. Otherwise, we're in danger of repeating the mistake.

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: I agree that we absolutely must take a long-term view. My point about 30 years was that it's difficult to reconstruct what decision-makers were thinking in the past, not that we shouldn't be planning 30 years into the future.

chapters.title: 2. How the government escaped the contract
chapters.takeaway: Court action, changes to rent arrangements and accounting rules helped the government negotiate a repurchase that officials say would previously have cost billions more.

turns.speaker: Chris Kane
turns.text: Why did it take nearly 25 years, until around 2019, for the Ministry of Defence to start seriously improving its position? Was someone trying to escape the deal throughout that period, or did the problem only receive attention much later?

turns.speaker: Mike Green
turns.text: Previous National Audit Office reports had identified problems, but we didn't have a strong enough position to bring Annington into serious negotiations. Three things changed that: successful court cases over our rights to acquire the properties, negotiations about rent, and new accounting rules. Together, they made a negotiated settlement possible.

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: One important change was IFRS 16. It meant the government had to record more of its future rental obligations as existing liabilities. Buying back the houses therefore didn't add the full purchase price to the government's recorded debt. That made the transaction easier to justify financially.

turns.speaker: David Brewer
turns.text: The financial damage from the original deal was growing rapidly. In comparable terms, the estimated loss increased from around £5.5 billion in 2018 to £8.5 billion six years later. We needed to act, but we also needed to create enough negotiating strength to get a sensible price.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: I understand that the eventual purchase price was much lower than Annington's valuation. But we'd spent decades paying under the original agreement and the houses were in poor condition. Why couldn't we have escaped sooner?

turns.speaker: David Brewer
turns.text: Because an earlier purchase could have cost billions more. The court action, rent negotiations and accounting changes were carefully planned steps that strengthened our position. Without them, we could have ended up paying an enormous premium to buy back properties from a company with much stronger negotiating power.

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: We ultimately paid £6 billion for homes valued at £10.1 billion on Annington's accounts. Our latest estimate is that buying them back will save the Ministry of Defence £7.7 billion over the next ten years. That doesn't excuse the original deal, but it shows the benefit of the work done to resolve it.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: This committee is often critical of your department, but the repurchase deserves recognition. I've checked the numbers myself, and I agree it was a good deal. The people involved should be congratulated.

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: I'm grateful for that. The successful repurchase also creates an opportunity to improve housing in ways the original contract made very difficult. We now need to make the most of that opportunity.

chapters.title: 3. The condition of military family homes
chapters.takeaway: Officials reported improvements in safety and complaints, but MPs pointed to poor repair services, outdated buildings and widespread dissatisfaction among military families.

turns.speaker: Matt Turmaine
turns.text: Let's turn to the homes themselves. After decades of poor maintenance, what are you doing to put things right?

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: This is a priority. We refurbished and redecorated 1,250 homes last year. Active complaints have fallen from around 4,200 in November 2022 to roughly 60 in July this year. Overall satisfaction with housing provided by the department has risen by 12 percentage points to 75%. That's encouraging, although we know many properties still aren't good enough.

turns.speaker: Mike Green
turns.text: When I arrived in 2022, I was shocked by the condition of the housing. We were providing homes with serious damp and mould problems, and some properties weren't meeting safety requirements. At the worst point, we had more than 4,000 cases of severe damp and mould. We've dealt with those cases and the major safety problems. But the underlying quality of the buildings is still poor.

turns.speaker: Matt Turmaine
turns.text: The National Audit Office's supporting figures tell a less encouraging story. Only 52% of families were satisfied with service family accommodation specifically. Satisfaction with responses to maintenance requests was 39%, compared with 45% dissatisfied. For the quality of repairs, just 33% were satisfied and 49% dissatisfied. Clearly there's still a long way to go.

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: Yes. The 75% figure I gave covers the wider range of housing provided by the department, not just family accommodation. We want much higher standards for our service personnel, and that requires sustained investment.

turns.speaker: Mike Green
turns.text: We've fixed the most urgent problems, but the buildings themselves need major work. Some have single-brick walls, poor insulation or ventilation that doesn't work properly. When energy is expensive, families keep windows closed and dry clothes indoors, making damp more likely. We can't solve those problems permanently just by responding to individual repair requests.

turns.speaker: Matt Turmaine
turns.text: How much of the housing is actually in good condition? Are we talking about a relatively small number of problem properties, or something much bigger?

turns.speaker: Mike Green
turns.text: About nine out of ten homes need significant attention. Roughly 90% meet the existing Decent Homes Standard, but that's only a minimum standard and doesn't necessarily mean they're homes people would be happy to live in. They've been underinvested in for 40 or 50 years. We need to move beyond making properties just tolerable.

turns.speaker: David Brewer
turns.text: Most of the estate was built between the end of the Second World War and the early 1970s. More than half the homes have an energy-efficiency rating worse than D on the A-to-G scale. We carry out around 250,000 repairs a year. That's a huge amount of disruption for families. We need to improve the buildings themselves while also giving people a better repair service in the meantime.

turns.speaker: Rupert Pearce
turns.text: We also need a different approach to maintenance. Historically, we often waited for something to break before fixing it. That can be more expensive in the long run. The ten-year investment programme should let us plan improvements ahead of time and use specialist expertise to prevent problems rather than constantly reacting to them.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: I'm still concerned about complacency. Satisfaction with family housing is actually worse than in 2012, when 56% were satisfied, compared with 52% now. Our personnel are sent overseas for long periods, sometimes on successive deployments, while their families live in poor housing. Why shouldn't military homes meet the same published standards expected of other publicly supported housing?

turns.speaker: Rupert Pearce
turns.text: I agree with that principle. We should provide standards comparable with what families could expect outside the military. There may need to be differences where military requirements make them necessary, but otherwise service life shouldn't mean accepting poorer housing. Good accommodation is essential if we're going to attract and keep the people our armed forces need.

chapters.title: 4. The money and the ten-year timetable
chapters.takeaway: The government says its £9.2 billion housing commitment remains protected, but £800 million has been delayed and MPs questioned whether improvements would come quickly enough.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You're talking about a ten-year programme, but that seems far too long when housing affects recruitment and whether people stay in the armed forces. Families can't reasonably be expected to endure poor conditions for another decade.

turns.speaker: David Brewer
turns.text: I don't want to suggest that families will wait ten years before seeing improvements. We're prioritising the worst properties and bringing forward work on their condition. The repair service and the standard of homes when people move in should also improve much sooner. Ten years is the period needed to address the underlying problems across the whole estate.

turns.speaker: Mike Green
turns.text: We're effectively facing the task of rebuilding or substantially improving tens of thousands of homes. We tackled around 1,000 of the worst properties last year and intend to do something similar this year. I wish there were a quick solution, but this is the result of decades of neglect. We now have an opportunity to put things right properly for the long term.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Let's establish exactly what money is available. The government has committed around £9 billion over ten years, but how much will actually be spent during this Parliament?

turns.speaker: Aneen Blackmore
turns.text: The commitment is £9.2 billion for service family accommodation over ten years, and that total remains protected. However, when balancing all the defence department's priorities, we had to move around £800 million of planned spending from this Parliament into the next one. Even with that change, we're planning increases in spending after inflation in each of the next three years.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The original additional allocation was around £1.5 billion, wasn't it? If you've delayed £800 million, does that mean you're only spending about £700 million during this Parliament? That sounds a long way from achieving £9.2 billion in ten years.

turns.speaker: Aneen Blackmore
turns.text: The £1.5 billion was an additional increase, not the total housing budget. Our current plan is to spend £2.7 billion on service family accommodation over the next four years. That figure already reflects the delayed spending. We remain committed to the full ten-year amount.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: I'm asking something simpler: how much will you spend on all military housing during this Parliament, and specifically this financial year? That includes accommodation for individual personnel as well as families. You must have a budget.

turns.speaker: Aneen Blackmore
turns.text: We do, but spending is recorded in several different parts of the department's budget. The figures I've given are for family housing, not single living accommodation or wider property improvement spending. I don't have the complete total with me, so I'll need to provide it in writing.

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: You've already written to me requesting those figures, and we'll respond by the deadline you've set. It's a fair question, and I accept that the committee needs a clear answer.

turns.speaker: Rupert Pearce
turns.text: We want better homes as quickly as possible, but housing competes for money and skilled workers with other urgent defence needs, including military equipment and readiness. It's one of our largest investment programmes. We're also exploring whether private partners can help us work faster, but it's too early to promise that they'll shorten the timetable.

chapters.title: 5. Building the right homes in the right places
chapters.takeaway: Owning the houses again should let the military replace unsuitable properties, improve existing ones and develop surplus land, although detailed plans and numbers are still being worked out.

turns.speaker: Matt Turmaine
turns.text: What specific progress can families expect over the next few years? Have you set targets for how many homes you'll improve?

turns.speaker: David Brewer
turns.text: We're examining the country in 65 areas, looking at how many homes we have, what sizes they are, where they're needed and what condition they're in. We're then comparing the costs of renovating, replacing or building homes. We're currently making around 1,000 substantial improvements a year, and I expect that rate to double. We also prepare 10,000 to 15,000 homes for families moving in each year, and we're raising the standard of that work.

turns.speaker: Rupert Pearce
turns.text: The difficulty isn't only the poor condition of the properties. We also have homes of the wrong size and type in the wrong places. We need to plan the estate around where military families actually need to live.

turns.speaker: David Brewer
turns.text: Under the Annington arrangement, we had very little flexibility to change where our houses were. Now that we own them, we can sell properties in places where they're no longer needed and buy or build in places where demand is greater. That's important because military requirements will continue to change.

turns.speaker: Matt Turmaine
turns.text: Will you also be able to buy suitable homes from ordinary housing developments rather than always building them yourselves?

turns.speaker: David Brewer
turns.text: Yes. Changes to planning policy mean military housing can qualify for certain affordable-housing arrangements, including homes provided through section 106 agreements. That gives us another way to obtain suitable properties at a reasonable cost. The Defence Housing Service will publish its plans and report annually on improvements and day-to-day service standards.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Do you know how many new homes you're likely to buy through those arrangements? Would it make sense to buy modern homes and sell older ones that would be expensive to repair?

turns.speaker: David Brewer
turns.text: We don't have a firm number yet. In some cases, replacing an old property will be better value, but our current analysis suggests we'll probably refurbish more homes than we buy. That depends on property prices and the cost of repairs, so we're still examining the options.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: There's also a government commitment to build homes on surplus defence land. How much land will you release, and how many homes will be built for the wider population?

turns.speaker: Rupert Pearce
turns.text: As part of the funding agreement, we've committed to making land and opportunities available for up to 100,000 new homes over the next ten years. That's an important part of the wider programme, alongside improving accommodation for military families.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: Are those homes intended for the ordinary housing market, or is there any connection with accommodation for asylum seekers, refugees or other migrants? I'd like that distinction to be completely transparent.

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: The stated objective is to build 100,000 homes for military use or the private housing market. The detailed strategy will be published by the Defence Housing Service in its first year. Separately, around 20% of existing family homes are currently empty, compared with what we'd regard as an ideal level of about 10%. Some vacancies are necessary because families move frequently and homes need preparing for new occupants.

turns.speaker: Mike Green
turns.text: A limited number of existing military homes have been used temporarily to accommodate Afghans under resettlement arrangements. I don't have the precise current number, but it's been falling as people move on. I can provide the figures in writing.

turns.speaker: Rupert Pearce
turns.text: My understanding is that the number remaining is now very small. The final temporary defence site used for the Afghan resettlement programme has closed. That's separate from the long-term programme to build new housing.

chapters.title: 6. Creating a new military housing organisation
chapters.takeaway: The Ministry of Defence is setting up a dedicated housing body, but MPs questioned whether it has enough specialist staff, independence and financial safeguards to succeed.

turns.speaker: Blake Stephenson
turns.text: The National Audit Office says the Ministry of Defence has little experience or expertise in property development, transforming housing areas or providing housing support services. Do you agree, and how will you overcome that problem?

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: That's one of the main reasons we're creating the Defence Housing Service. We're recruiting specialists in property development, construction, buying and selling homes, and housing management. Natalie Elphicke has been appointed chair, and we're recruiting additional board members. We need an organisation that can manage property professionally and treat service personnel and their families as customers.

turns.speaker: Blake Stephenson
turns.text: But do you actually have those skills now? The National Audit Office specifically questions your experience in housing support, not just property development.

turns.speaker: Mike Green
turns.text: We do have considerable experience in looking after housing because we're already one of the UK's largest housing providers. We maintain properties and provide services, even if we haven't always done that well or had enough money. I accept that property development is different. Those are skills we need to bring into the organisation.

turns.speaker: Blake Stephenson
turns.text: What will the new organisation cost, how independent will it be, and how can we be sure it won't repeat the department's past problems?

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: It's already operating in a preparatory form, but its formal establishment depends on Parliament passing the Armed Forces Bill. We're aiming for 1 April 2027, provided we can do so safely, protect public money and serve military families properly. The arrangements for its management and oversight are still being developed, and some decisions will be for ministers.

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: The department will be able to use money raised by selling properties. The new organisation will also have legal powers to borrow, but we have no plans for it to borrow to fund military housing. Borrowing might eventually support commercial developments with private partners, but that would require Treasury agreement. Nothing has been approved on that front.

turns.speaker: Blake Stephenson
turns.text: Given all the competing demands on defence spending, are you confident the new service will actually receive enough funding to get started properly?

turns.speaker: Rupert Pearce
turns.text: Yes. I'm confident the agreed defence spending plan contains the funding needed for the organisation and its ambitions. We still have to turn those commitments into detailed programmes, but the government's support is there. Having a dedicated public body should also help us attract specialists, work with partners and respond more quickly.

turns.speaker: David Brewer
turns.text: We've developed plans for the professional staff and resources needed to establish the organisation, and those costs are included in the agreed funding. We're confident we can build the capability required, although the detailed housing programme is still being finalised.

chapters.title: 7. Working with private companies without repeating past mistakes
chapters.takeaway: Officials argued that expert advice and carefully structured partnerships can protect taxpayers, while MPs warned against taking unnecessary commercial risks or repeating the mistakes of 1996.

turns.speaker: Blake Stephenson
turns.text: One positive finding in the audit report was how effectively you used UK Government Investments during the repurchase. What should other government departments learn from that experience?

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: Their advice was invaluable. My recommendation is to involve specialists from UK Government Investments early, while decisions are still being shaped, rather than bringing them in at the end. We also benefited from close cooperation with the Treasury and clear direction from ministers. That combination helped us negotiate a good outcome.

turns.speaker: Mike Green
turns.text: When you're negotiating over billions of pounds, you need people who really understand the numbers. UK Government Investments helped us work out what a reasonable price would be and gave us confidence about how far we could go in negotiations. We also used legal specialists, but we didn't spend vast sums hiring an investment bank to run the deal.

turns.speaker: David Brewer
turns.text: The important lesson was how we worked with those experts. We didn't simply ask consultants to produce reports and then review them separately. We built one team, with our own commercial specialists working directly alongside the advisers. That meant we could make decisions quickly and knew when we needed additional expertise.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: I have a serious concern about the new housing service becoming a property developer in its own right. Building homes for the commercial market isn't the Ministry of Defence's main job. Competing against experienced private developers could distract the department and expose taxpayers to enormous losses.

turns.speaker: Rupert Pearce
turns.text: I agree with the concern in principle. I want the Defence Housing Service to work in partnership with experienced developers, not try to compete directly against them. We should use their skills where they're stronger than ours, rather than assuming we can build all that expertise ourselves.

turns.speaker: David Brewer
turns.text: We don't intend to become a competing housebuilder. We've already worked successfully with private developers, including Urban&Civic at Waterbeach. Developers have also suggested that, by working with us on surplus land, they could help us buy materials such as windows, doors, kitchens and bathrooms more cheaply for military housing improvements. Those activities could benefit each other.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: Coming back to the original £14.5 billion loss, isn't the fundamental lesson that governments shouldn't make deals that look cheap today but leave taxpayers facing huge costs later? Private companies will naturally try to get the best possible terms. How can government stop itself being taken advantage of?

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: I agree that the original deal placed too much emphasis on immediate financial returns. We need to be much more careful about the incentives contracts create. If each side benefits from completely different outcomes, problems can follow. The better approach is to make their interests work together where possible. I should also say that colleagues involved in the recent repurchase told me Annington acted professionally during negotiations.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: When I see a contract that looks exceptionally bad for one party, I wonder whether something more serious has gone wrong, potentially even fraud or improper conduct. Does the department investigate how such deals were reached, rather than simply moving on?

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: We do scrutinise our decisions and try to learn from them. This particular arrangement has been examined repeatedly by the National Audit Office. I'm not going to speculate further about the concerns you've raised.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The committee has previously examined fraud and errors in the Ministry of Defence, so we know those checks matter. For today, we recognise the achievement of ending this expensive contract. The next challenge is to improve military housing as quickly as possible. Service personnel and their families make enormous sacrifices, and providing decent homes is essential if we're going to recruit and retain the people our armed forces need.
